views.name: product_monthly_sales
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  product_id,
  mth,
  SUM(qty) AS qty
FROM monthly_sales
GROUP BY product_id, mth

params.when_to_use: Calculating total quantity sold for a specific product in a specific month (e.g., "How many units of product X were sold in 2023-05?"). | Building month-by-month time series of sales volume per product (e.g., trend charts, month-over-month growth) where the desired granularity is product × month. | Joining to product-level attributes when you need the monthly quantity as an aggregate metric (e.g., attach monthly qty to product records for reporting). | Feeding downstream aggregations that explicitly re-aggregate from product × month to higher grains (e.g., roll up to product-year or product across all months) and where SUM of the monthly qty is correct.
params.when_not_to_use: Answering questions at a finer grain than product × month (e.g., per-order-line, per-order, per-customer). The view has been aggregated and loses row-level identifiers; you cannot reconstruct order-level or line-level detail — using it will silently undercount or hide heterogeneity. | Computing metrics that depend on distinct counts of lower-level entities (orders, customers, SKUs per order). Because the view only stores summed qty, DISTINCT counts or averages per order/customer cannot be derived correctly and will produce wrong results silently. | Filtering by cohorts that are defined at a different grain (for example: "orders placed in a month" or "customers active in a month"). The view aggregates quantity by product and month and does not preserve which orders or customers contributed; cohort membership cannot be applied reliably after aggregation. | Joining expecting non-aggregated attributes from monthly_sales (e.g., order_id, customer_id, store_id). Those columns are not present; attempts to join as if they existed will fail or produce incorrect multiplicative results if you try to re-join to monthly_sales to recover details. | Using this view to compute averages or rates that require denominators from a different grain (e.g., avg qty per order in a month). Since the view lacks order counts, dividing SUM(qty) by something inferred from this view will be incorrect unless you obtain correct denominators separately. | Creating windows/lead/lag at a sub-month granularity or per-order sequence. The view’s grain is per-month — intra-month sequencing and windowing across lower-level rows are impossible.
params.comparison: use product_total_sales(AGG) instead when you need totals aggregated across all months (product-level only) — it has the same aggregation intent but different grain (product_total_sales likely aggregates only by product, while product_monthly_sales is product × month). | use orders_with_lines(JOIN) when you need order-level or order-line-level detail (order_id, line_id, customer context) — orders_with_lines preserves lower-level identifiers and joinable columns that product_monthly_sales does not. | use purchases_enriched(JOIN) or inventory_with_locations(JOIN) when you need contextual fields about purchases or inventory locations alongside quantities — those sibling JOIN views retain non-aggregated attributes and richer dimension data that this aggregated view has removed. | use web_daily_devices(NORM) or web_demographics_unpivot(RESHAPE) when your analysis concerns user/web signals at their native grain — those siblings preserve the original per-day or per-person records rather than summing them into product × month. | use orders_latest_by_customer(RANK) or picking_activity_window(WIN) when you require ranking/window logic or temporal windows at the event/order level — product_monthly_sales cannot reproduce ranking/window semantics because it’s already aggregated. | use product_reorder_guidance(SEM) when you want recommended reorder quantities or semantic guidance derived from multiple signals — product_monthly_sales only provides raw monthly qty and lacks the model/heuristic outputs.

views.description: Aggregated monthly sales per product. Use this when you need total quantity sold by product and month (time series, budgeting comparisons, trend analysis). | Use for: monthly sales trends for a product; compare actual sales to budget by month; time series joins to product attributes

views.name: product_total_sales
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  product_id,
  SUM(qty) AS qty_total
FROM monthly_sales
GROUP BY product_id

params.when_to_use: Report total quantity sold per product across all available months in monthly_sales — e.g., “What is the lifetime (or dataset-wide) total qty sold for each product?” | Joining product-level totals to a products table to show overall sales per product (one row per product_id). | Downstream aggregation or ranking that needs a single scalar total per product (e.g., top-N products by total qty).
params.when_not_to_use: Any question that requires time granularity (monthly/daily): this view collapses time by summing over all months in monthly_sales, so it will silently remove the temporal dimension and cannot answer “qty per product per month”. | Analyses that require additional transaction/context columns from monthly_sales (e.g., store_id, date, order_id): those details are lost because the view groups only by product_id, so joining back to this view will misrepresent row-level or segment-level counts. | Cohort or filtered counts based on a subset of months (e.g., last 12 months): the view contains the total across all months present in monthly_sales; reusing it without re-filtering will overcount for time-bounded cohorts. | Calculations that need distinct counts of orders or lines (e.g., number of orders containing the product): summing qty is not the same as counting distinct order_ids; reuse would produce incorrect metrics. | Cases that need inventory or purchase-side quantities (inventory, purchases): this view is sales-only (sums qty from monthly_sales) and will mislead if used to represent on-hand, purchased, or replenished quantities.
params.comparison: use product_monthly_sales(AGG) instead when you need the same metric but broken out by month — it has the same source but preserves the monthly grain rather than aggregating across time. | use products_with_group(JOIN) or products_with_alcohol(JOIN) when you need product attributes (group, alcohol flag) alongside quantities — those sibling joins provide product metadata that this view does not include. | use orders_with_lines(JOIN) when you need order-level or line-level context (order_id, line_id) for counts or per-order metrics — that view retains the transactional grain unlike this product-level aggregate. | use inventory_with_locations(JOIN) or purchases_enriched(JOIN) when comparing sales to inventory or purchase quantities — those views represent different lifecycle aspects (inventory/purchases) and preserve relevant location or supplier dimensions. | use product_reorder_guidance(SEM) when you need reorder signals or forecasted reorder quantities — that semantic view incorporates business logic beyond historical sales totals and should be used for replenishment decisions.

views.description: Total sales quantity per product across all months. Useful for ranking top-selling products, computing lifetime sales, or joining to product metadata. | Use for: top N products by sales; product-level lifetime sales for reporting; join lifetime sales to product groups or alcohol properties

views.name: products_with_group
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  p.id AS id,
  p.name AS name,
  p.group_id AS group_id,
  pg.name AS name__group
FROM products p
LEFT JOIN product_groups pg ON p.group_id = pg.id

params.when_to_use: Get the canonical product row attributes (id, name, group_id) along with the product group name for each product id. | Display a product catalog, product detail page, or admin list where one row per product (product.id) is required. | Join product-level events or metrics (that are already at product grain) to enrich them with group name without changing row counts.
params.when_not_to_use: Aggregate sales or metrics across time or orders — this view is at product grain, not aggregated. Using it directly to answer questions like 'total sales per product per month' will miss required grouping and can silently under/over-count (use an AGG view or aggregate after joining): it has one row per product, not one row per product×month or per order. | Compute cohort or time-windowed metrics (e.g., monthly, daily, rolling windows) — the view contains no time or transactional columns, so joining it into time-based analyses can produce duplicated rows if the other side is at a finer grain. | Measure order- or line-level metrics (e.g., revenue per order line) — because products_with_group is one row per product, joining it to orders/lines without careful keys can inflate counts if the join to order lines produces multiple rows per product. | Use as a source of product availability or inventory status — it has no inventory, location, or stock columns; using it instead of inventory_with_locations or purchases_enriched will miss those fields and may produce incorrect conclusions. | Assume completeness of group information for filtering cohorts — group_id can be NULL (LEFT JOIN preserves products without a group); filtering on name__group without accounting for NULLs can drop intended products.
params.comparison: use product_total_sales instead when you need per-product aggregated sales (it is AGG) — products_with_group is at product row grain and lacks aggregated metrics. | use product_monthly_sales instead when you need time-bucketed sales by product (it is AGG by month) — products_with_group has no date or monthly aggregation. | use products_with_alcohol instead when you need a filtered product subset (it is a JOIN that likely restricts or annotates alcohol products) — products_with_group includes all products and does not apply that domain filter. | use orders_with_lines when joining to order-level or line-level data — orders_with_lines has the transactional context needed to avoid accidental duplication when computing order metrics; products_with_group only provides product attributes. | use inventory_with_locations or purchases_enriched when you need stock, location, or procurement attributes — those sibling JOIN views include inventory/purchase fields that products_with_group does not. | use orders_latest_by_customer or picking_activity_window when you need ranked or windowed, time-scoped slices of operational data — products_with_group does not provide ranking/window columns and is static product metadata.

views.description: Denormalized product rows with their product group name. Use when you need product attributes together with group metadata for reporting or joins. | Use for: list products with their group names; aggregate sales by product group by joining to this CTE; filter products by group attributes

views.name: products_with_alcohol
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  p.id AS id,
  p.name AS name,
  p.group_id AS group_id,
  pa.sales_volume AS sales_volume,
  pa.abv AS abv
FROM products p
LEFT JOIN product_alcohol pa ON p.id = pa.product_id

params.when_to_use: When you need a row-per-product (grain = product.id) record that includes the product's alcohol attributes (abv and sales_volume) as stored in the product_alcohol table, i.e., product detail queries such as 'show products with their ABV and the corresponding product_alcohol.sales_volume value'. | When you want to join product-level data to other tables (e.g., enrich orders or inventory) and require the product-level alcohol fields attached to each product id. | When you need to display or export the canonical product attributes: id, name, group_id together with the product_alcohol fields, and you expect NULL product_alcohol values for products that have no matching product_alcohol row (LEFT JOIN semantics).
params.when_not_to_use: Do not use this view to compute aggregated sales totals, trends, or time series (e.g., 'monthly sales by product' or 'total sales by product across time'): the view is at product.id grain and returns product_alcohol.sales_volume as-is, so aggregating without understanding its source or time dimension can double-count or misrepresent time-based metrics. | Do not use this view to answer questions about sales at a different grain (orders, order lines, months, stores): it is not normalized to order/line/month grains and will silently lose or misattribute rows when used as if it were at an event or time grain. | Do not use this view when you need only products that have alcohol metadata and want to drop non-alcohol products unless you explicitly filter (the view uses LEFT JOIN and will return products with NULL abv/sales_volume). Reusing it without filtering will include non-alcohol products and produce incorrect cohorts. | Do not use this view to infer completeness of product_alcohol data (e.g., 'count of alcohol-tagged products'): because this view preserves one row per product, it cannot show cases where product_alcohol has multiple rows per product_id — those would be lost if JOIN cardinality is assumed unique elsewhere. | Do not use this view if you require validated uniqueness or referential assumptions about product_alcohol (the view assumes product.id is unique but does not enforce that product_alcohol is 0/1 rows per product; if product_alcohol has multiple rows, the LEFT JOIN produces multiple output rows per product leading to unexpected duplicates when downstream logic assumes strict 1:1).
params.comparison: use product_total_sales instead when you need aggregated sales totals per product — product_total_sales is an AGG view that summarizes sales rather than exposing the raw product_alcohol.sales_volume field. | use product_monthly_sales instead when you need time-bucketed (monthly) sales per product — product_monthly_sales is an AGG view at the (product, month) grain rather than product.id grain. | use products_with_group instead when you only need product and group metadata without alcohol fields — products_with_group is a JOIN sibling focused on grouping metadata and avoids bringing in product_alcohol, so it's safer when alcohol attributes are irrelevant. | use orders_with_lines or orders_latest_by_customer when your question is about orders or order-lines (event grain) rather than product-level attributes — those JOIN/RANK views are at the order/line/customer-event grains and preserve event-level cardinality. | use inventory_with_locations or purchases_enriched when your focus is on inventory or purchase transactions that include location/transaction context — those JOIN views maintain transaction/location grains that this product-level view does not. | use web_daily_devices or web_demographics_unpivot when working with normalized/reshaped web analytics data — those sibling views are specifically normalized/reshaped for web event analyses rather than product attributes. | use picking_activity_window, employee_supervision_paths, or product_reorder_guidance when your question relates to windowed activity, hierarchical relationships, or reorder recommendations — those specialized views implement different logic (WINDOW/REC/SEM) and different grains than products_with_alcohol.

views.description: Products joined to alcohol properties (sales_volume, abv). Useful for analyses that need alcohol attributes next to product identifiers. | Use for: compare sales by ABV; filter products by alcohol strength; enrich sales/inventory with ABV for reporting

views.name: orders_with_lines
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  ol.id AS id,
  ol.order_id AS order_id,
  ol.product_id AS product_id,
  ol.qty AS qty,
  ol.amount AS amount,
  o.customer_id AS customer_id,
  o.ordered AS ordered,
  o.delivery AS delivery
FROM orderlines ol
LEFT JOIN orders o ON ol.order_id = o.id

params.when_to_use: Get one row per order line with its parent order attributes — e.g., list order lines with qty, amount, and the order's customer_id, ordered timestamp, or delivery info. | Join orderline-level events to other line-level or product-level tables (product_id, inventory or product dimension) where you need the order-level context on each line. | Compute metrics that are naturally at the order-line grain (line counts, line-level revenue = amount, average qty per line) where each physical orderline should be counted separately.
params.when_not_to_use: When you need aggregates at the order grain (one row per order) — this view is at the orderline grain (ol.id). Reusing it and then grouping by order_id without careful aggregation will double-count or over-count if you expect one row per order. | When you need an accurate customer-level cohort or lifetime metrics: using this view directly will produce multiple rows per customer (one per orderline) and will require explicit deduplication (e.g., DISTINCT order_id or customer-level aggregation) to avoid inflated counts. | When you need only orders (some orders have no orderlines): because this is a LEFT JOIN from orderlines to orders, orders that have no orderlines are absent. Reusing the view to answer "orders that meet X" will miss orders without lines. | When you need to guarantee no NULL order attributes: the view preserves order columns from a LEFT JOIN; if there exist orderlines referencing missing orders, customer_id/ordered/delivery can be NULL. Using the view assuming those columns are always populated can lead to silently wrong results. | When you need the latest order per customer (or other row-level deduplication by time): this view returns every orderline, not a ranked/latest row per order or customer. Use a ranking or latest-by view instead to avoid multiple matches. | When you need pre-aggregated product sales totals or monthly summaries: this join emits detail rows that will have to be aggregated; reusing without proper GROUP BY and aggregation expressions will produce incorrect totals or counts.
params.comparison: use orders_latest_by_customer(RANK) instead when you need one order (or order attribute snapshot) per customer — orders_with_lines has many rows per customer and no ranking/deduplication. | use product_monthly_sales(AGG) or product_total_sales(AGG) instead when you need pre-aggregated product revenue or monthly rollups — orders_with_lines is row-level and will require grouping and careful SUM/DATE_TRUNC to avoid mis-aggregation. | use products_with_group(JOIN) or products_with_alcohol(JOIN) when you need enriched product attributes joined at product grain — orders_with_lines contains product_id per line but is not focused on product dimension joins or product-level uniqueness. | use inventory_with_locations(JOIN) when you need inventory-location level information — orders_with_lines is sales/orderline focused and does not provide inventory location context. | use purchases_enriched(JOIN) or product_reorder_guidance(SEM) when your question is about procurement/reordering heuristics — orders_with_lines is sales data and may mislead reorder calculations unless aggregated appropriately by product and time.

views.description: Order lines joined to their parent orders and customers. One row per orderline with order-level context (ordered date, customer). Useful for revenue, fulfillment, and customer purchase history queries. | Use for: customer purchase history; order line level revenue/time analysis; fulfillment and delivery timing queries

views.name: inventory_with_locations
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  i.id AS id,
  i.location_id AS location_id,
  i.product_id AS product_id,
  i.purchase_id AS purchase_id,
  i.qty AS qty,
  l.warehouse AS warehouse,
  l.aisle AS aisle,
  l.position AS position
FROM inventory i
LEFT JOIN locations l ON i.location_id = l.id

params.when_to_use: Get inventory rows with their canonical location attributes for each inventory.id — use when you need one record per inventory row (grain = inventory.id). | Enrich inventory-level analyses with location details (warehouse, aisle, position) without changing row counts — e.g., show qty by inventory id and location. | Join inventory rows to other tables at the inventory row level (e.g., to trace a specific inventory record to a location). | Export or display detailed inventory rows including product_id and purchase_id along with their physical location.
params.when_not_to_use: Do not use when you need aggregated inventory totals (per product, per warehouse, per purchase): this view is row-level and will double-count if aggregated incorrectly (aggregation must GROUP BY inventory.id or other keys). | Avoid using it to answer cohort or time-window questions (e.g., ‘inventory as of date’, ‘monthly stock levels’): the view has no time dimension and provides current inventory rows only. | Do not use as a substitute for product- or purchase-level views — using it to compute product totals without grouping by product_id will produce mis-counted sums because the view is at inventory.id grain. | Avoid using for presence/absence counts (distinct products or locations) unless you explicitly distinct on the correct column — LEFT JOIN preserves inventory rows even when location is NULL, which can mislead counts of locations. | Do not reuse when you need only location entities (warehouse/aisle/position) independent of inventory rows — this view couples locations to inventory and will omit locations with no inventory and include inventory rows with NULL location fields.
params.comparison: use product_monthly_sales(AGG) instead when you need aggregated sales per product per month — it is already aggregated by time and product and avoids manual grouping of inventory rows. | use product_total_sales(AGG) instead when you need total sales per product across time — product_total_sales provides correct aggregation at product grain rather than the inventory.id grain. | use products_with_group(JOIN) or products_with_alcohol(JOIN) instead when your question is about product attributes or categorizations independent of inventory rows — those sibling joins attach product-level attributes and avoid inventory-level duplication. | use orders_with_lines(JOIN) or purchases_enriched(JOIN) when you need purchase/order-centric analyses — those are built at the purchase/order grain and are appropriate for order-level aggregation, whereas inventory_with_locations is at inventory.id and includes purchase_id only as an attribute. | use orders_latest_by_customer(RANK) when you need the most recent order per customer — ranking logic is handled there; inventory_with_locations has no ranking or date logic. | use web_daily_devices(NORM) or web_demographics_unpivot(RESHAPE) for web-analytics-shaped data — inventory_with_locations is unrelated and will not provide normalized or unpivoted web metrics. | use picking_activity_window(WIN) for windowed picking activity metrics — that view contains window functions and temporal logic that inventory_with_locations lacks. | use product_reorder_guidance(SEM) when you need reorder recommendations — that semantic guidance is computed at product/warehouse granularity and accounts for demand; inventory_with_locations is raw inventory rows.

views.description: Inventory rows enriched with location attributes (warehouse, aisle, position). Use for stock location reporting, picking optimizations, and spatial inventory analyses. | Use for: where is stock located for a product; aggregate inventory by warehouse/aisle; optimize picking by location

views.name: purchases_enriched
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  p.id AS id,
  p.purchased AS purchased,
  p.brewery_id AS brewery_id,
  p.product_id AS product_id,
  p.qty AS qty,
  p.cost AS cost,
  b.name AS name__brewery,
  pr.name AS name__product
FROM purchases p
LEFT JOIN breweries b ON p.brewery_id = b.id
LEFT JOIN products pr ON p.product_id = pr.id

params.when_to_use: Answer questions about individual purchase line records (one row per purchase id) such as: show the purchase timestamp, quantity, cost, product id, and brewery for a specific purchase id or set of purchase ids. | Join back to other row-level tables keyed by purchases.id to enrich or filter individual purchase events. | List purchases with human-readable product and brewery names when you need the full row-level detail (e.g., display recent purchases or audit a specific transaction). | Filter by product_id, brewery_id, purchased timestamp, or exact qty/cost at the purchase-row level.
params.when_not_to_use: Do NOT use for aggregated reporting (sums, counts, averages) over products, breweries, or time without first aggregating at the correct level — this view is at purchase-row grain, so aggregating it naively can double-count when there are multiple lines per order or when joining to other entities. | Do NOT use for product-level or brewery-level metrics (e.g., total sales per product or per month) — use an aggregation view instead because this view contains individual purchase rows rather than pre-aggregated totals; using it directly for those metrics may require GROUP BY and careful deduplication. | Do NOT use as a cohort or customer-level source (e.g., unique customers who purchased a product) because it is at purchase id grain and may contain multiple purchases per customer; deduplicating by customer is required before answering customer-cohort questions. | Do NOT use when the desired grain is orders or order lines if orders and purchases have different identifiers or cardinality — if there is an orders table with multiple lines per order, this view will not represent order-level totals. | Do NOT use for time-windowed analyses that expect pre-rolled windows (e.g., 'monthly sales') — use the time-aggregated sibling views to avoid mistakes in binning and aggregation.
params.comparison: use product_monthly_sales (AGG) instead when you need time-bucketed, pre-aggregated sales per product — it already aggregates purchases into monthly totals, avoiding row-level double-counting and manual GROUP BY. | use product_total_sales (AGG) instead when you need overall aggregated sales per product across the dataset — it provides product-level totals rather than individual purchase rows. | use products_with_group (JOIN) instead when you need product metadata enriched with group/category information — that sibling focuses on product-centric joins, whereas purchases_enriched is purchase-centric. | use products_with_alcohol (JOIN) instead when you need product attributes related to alcohol content for product-level filtering — purchases_enriched only brings product name, not alcohol attributes. | use orders_with_lines (JOIN) instead when you need order-level structure with its order lines — orders_with_lines represents orders and their line items, which may differ in grain or identifiers from purchases_enriched. | use inventory_with_locations (JOIN) when you need inventory quantities by location — purchases_enriched does not contain inventory location or stock-level data. | use web_daily_devices (NORM) or web_demographics_unpivot (RESHAPE) for web analytics shapes — those siblings are normalized/reshaped specifically for web event analysis, unlike the purchase-row join here. | use orders_latest_by_customer (RANK) when you need last-order-per-customer logic — purchases_enriched is not deduplicated by customer and will include all purchase rows. | use picking_activity_window (WIN) when you need windowed activity summaries (e.g., rolling windows) — purchases_enriched is raw row data without window calculations. | use employee_supervision_paths (REC) when exploring hierarchical employee relationships — unrelated grain and purpose compared with purchase rows. | use product_reorder_guidance (SEM) when you want reorder recommendations and thresholds — that sibling encodes business logic for reorder points, whereas purchases_enriched only supplies raw purchase rows and names.

views.description: Purchases with brewery and product metadata (product name, brewery name). Useful for supplier spend analysis and product-level costing. | Use for: supplier costing over time; purchase quantities by product; join purchases to sales for margin analysis

views.name: web_daily_devices
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  day,
  pc,
  tablet,
  phone,
  (COALESCE(pc,0) + COALESCE(tablet,0) + COALESCE(phone,0)) AS total_devices
FROM web_devices

params.when_to_use: Report or chart that needs counts of devices present per calendar day (one row per day) — i.e., daily device totals broken out by device type (pc, tablet, phone) and the summed total_devices. | Simple trend analysis of device counts over time at the day grain (e.g., 30‑day rolling average of total_devices), where no additional filtering or join logic is required. | Downstream calculations that require the raw per‑day device counts exactly as recorded in web_devices (no repartitioning, no additional deduplication). | Exporting or QC checks that compare aggregated sums from web_devices to the per‑day breakdown to validate upstream ingestion.
params.when_not_to_use: When you need device counts for a different grain (hourly, weekly, monthly, per session, per user). This view is strictly daily; aggregating it up to another grain may double‑count or misalign if web_devices already represents a different logical unit. | When you need device counts scoped to a cohort (e.g., per customer, per country, per product). This view contains no join keys or cohort columns, so filtering after joining may produce incorrect row counts or unintentionally change denominators. | When you need distinct device counts deduplicated by another entity (e.g., unique devices per user or per session). The view exposes whatever counts are in web_devices; it does not perform deduplication, so reuse for uniqueness questions can silently overcount. | When you need device metrics that depend on event-level detail (session duration, event timestamps finer than day). This view only contains the aggregated daily counts and cannot answer event‑level questions accurately. | When you expect NULL handling other than COALESCE-to-zero. The view coerces NULLs to 0 only in the computed total_devices expression; if downstream logic needs to preserve NULL semantics for pc/tablet/phone, reusing this view may mask missing data. | When combining with other aggregated views without matching grains and aggregation logic. Reusing this view in joins or unions with non-daily or differently-aggregated datasets can produce silently wrong aggregates (wrong denominators, double counts).
params.comparison: use web_demographics_unpivot instead when you need device counts by demographic buckets — web_demographics_unpivot is a reshape intended for per‑attribute breakdowns, whereas web_daily_devices only provides totals by device type at the day grain. | use orders_with_lines instead when you need device counts tied to order or line-item data — orders_with_lines is a JOIN that associates order context, while web_daily_devices has no order keys or commerce context. | use orders_latest_by_customer when your question is customer‑centric (e.g., devices used by each customer's latest order) — that view is ranked per customer and preserves customer-level logic; web_daily_devices is purely day-level aggregation. | use product_monthly_sales or product_total_sales when you need device metrics correlated to product sales at monthly or total aggregation — those AGG sibling views match different grains/aggregation and include sales context that web_daily_devices lacks. | use purchases_enriched or purchases_enriched-like JOIN views when you need device counts scoped to purchase events or enriched purchase attributes — web_daily_devices lacks event joins and will not correctly attribute devices to purchases.

views.description: Canonical daily device counts with a derived total column. Use for device-share calculations and joining to other daily web metrics. | Use for: device share per day; trend of overall device counts; join devices to web demographics or page visits by day

views.name: web_demographics_unpivot
views.body_sql:
SELECT day, 'M' AS gender_letter, 'tw' AS channel_shortcut, m_tw_cnt AS measure_cnt, m_tw_qty AS measure_qty FROM web_demographics
UNION ALL
SELECT day, 'M' AS gender_letter, 'fb' AS channel_shortcut, m_fb_cnt AS measure_cnt, m_fb_qty AS measure_qty FROM web_demographics
UNION ALL
SELECT day, 'F' AS gender_letter, 'tw' AS channel_shortcut, f_tw_cnt AS measure_cnt, f_tw_qty AS measure_qty FROM web_demographics
UNION ALL
SELECT day, 'F' AS gender_letter, 'fb' AS channel_shortcut, f_fb_cnt AS measure_cnt, f_fb_qty AS measure_qty FROM web_demographics

params.when_to_use: Calculate daily counts or quantities broken down by gender (M/F) and channel (tw/fb) exactly as stored in web_demographics: e.g., “What were the m_tw_cnt, m_tw_qty, f_tw_cnt, f_tw_qty broken out per day as rows?” — use this view to reshape those four column pairs into rows. | Build time series or charts at the daily × gender × channel grain using the pre-aggregated measures (measure_cnt, measure_qty) coming directly from web_demographics. | Join this view when you need a compact long-form table of the existing precomputed channel×gender measures for filtering, plotting, or simple aggregates that respect the same aggregation level (day × gender × channel).
params.when_not_to_use: When you need individual-level or event-level rows (session, user, or request): this view contains aggregated counts/quantities per day/gender/channel, so reusing it for row-level analyses will silently undercount or be meaningless. | When you need a different time grain (e.g., hourly, weekly, monthly): the view is daily; aggregating it to a coarser grain might be valid, but using it as though it contains finer-grained data (hourly) is incorrect and will produce misleading results. | When you need other genders or channels beyond the four encoded combinations (M/F × tw/fb): the view hardcodes 'M'/'F' and 'tw'/'fb' and will not include unknown/other categories, so reusing it will omit cohorts. | When you need measures that are derived differently (e.g., distinct user counts, rates, averages, or measures computed across joins): measure_cnt and measure_qty are copied from specific web_demographics columns and are not raw events — reusing them for different measure semantics will silently produce wrong analytics. | When you need to compare sibling views by aggregation semantics: this view reshapes columns into rows without recomputing or normalizing values. If you need normalized device-level rows or enriched order/product joins, use the appropriate sibling (see comparison).
params.comparison: use web_daily_devices instead when you need device-level (normalized) rows or to join to device identifiers — web_demographics (and this view) provides only aggregated counts/quantities and cannot be joined to device-level dimensions. | use product_monthly_sales or product_total_sales when your question is about product-level sales aggregates (monthly or total) — this view has a different subject (web demographics) and different aggregation semantics (daily gender×channel counts), so it is not interchangeable. | use purchases_enriched or orders_with_lines when you require row-level transaction/order detail or enriched purchase attributes — those siblings provide joins to transactional data and line-level measures, whereas this view provides only pre-aggregated day×gender×channel metrics. | use orders_latest_by_customer or picking_activity_window when you need ranking, windowed or latest-per-key logic — this view contains no rank/window logic and reusing it would lose those semantics. | use products_with_group or products_with_alcohol when you need product categorical enrichment — this view contains no product dimension data and cannot substitute for product joins.

views.description: Unpivots daily web demographics into one row per day x gender x channel x measure (cnt vs qty). Useful for flexible aggregations and joins to channel/gender dimensions. | Use for: compare channels by gender; time series of counts vs quantities per segment; join to channels_dim or gender_dim for labels

views.name: orders_latest_by_customer
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  o.id AS id,
  o.customer_id AS customer_id,
  o.ordered AS ordered,
  o.delivery AS delivery,
  ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY o.customer_id ORDER BY o.ordered DESC) AS rn_order_by_customer
FROM orders o

params.when_to_use: Get the latest order per customer (one row per order id, with a row-number that identifies the newest order for that customer). Example question: "Which order is each customer's most recent order?" — use rows where rn_order_by_customer = 1. | Identify or join the most-recent order per customer into another dataset when you will filter on rn_order_by_customer = 1 (or otherwise explicitly use rn_order_by_customer to pick a rank). | Debug or inspect ordering behavior by customer: compare timestamps (ordered) across a single customer's orders or validate ordering logic (ORDER BY ordered DESC). | Produce a dataset at the raw orders grain (one row per orders.id) that includes a per-customer rank used downstream to choose a single order per customer.
params.when_not_to_use: As an aggregated per-customer summary (e.g., total number of orders, total spend per customer). WHY: This view is still at the orders.id grain (one row per order) and does not aggregate; using it instead of a true aggregation will double-count orders when you group by customer. | As a replacement for a single-row-per-customer table without filtering to rn_order_by_customer = 1. WHY: The view contains all orders for every customer with a rank; failing to filter leaves multiple rows per customer and will produce wrong cohorts or counts. | To compute time-windowed/top-N orders without re-evaluating the window in the desired frame. WHY: The window uses ORDER BY ordered DESC across all history; if you need 'latest within the last 30 days' or other windowed semantics, this view's rank is computed across all orders and will be silently incorrect. | To represent a cohort of customers (e.g., customers active in a date range) unless you apply appropriate filters on ordered/delivery. WHY: The view does not filter by date or activity — presence of rn_order_by_customer does not imply cohort membership. | As a source for order-line level metrics or itemized revenue. WHY: The view lacks line-level columns; joining it in place of an orders_with_lines or similar join will lose or miscount line items. | When you need a stable, materialized "latest order" snapshot that won't change if new orders arrive. WHY: This view computes ROW_NUMBER() at query time, so the identity of rn_order_by_customer = 1 can change as new orders are inserted.
params.comparison: use orders_with_lines instead when you need order lines, item-level quantities, or to compute order revenue by summing lines — orders_latest_by_customer has the same orders grain but lacks line data (JOIN vs RANK). | use product_total_sales or product_monthly_sales when you need aggregated sales numbers by product (total or monthly) — those are AGG views and summarize across orders; orders_latest_by_customer is at order-id grain and provides no aggregation. | use purchases_enriched when you need enriched purchase/payer metadata or normalized purchaser-level attributes — purchases_enriched is a JOIN/ENRICHED view intended for cohort/attribution work, while orders_latest_by_customer only provides per-order rows with a per-customer rank. | use product_reorder_guidance when making product-level replenishment decisions — that view is SEM/analysis-focused on product reorder signals; orders_latest_by_customer is focused on order instances and per-customer recency. | use web_daily_devices or web_demographics_unpivot for web/device-level user segmentation or normalized demographic facts — those are NORM/RESHAPE views serving different grains and purposes; mixing them with this view without careful joins/filters will mismatch grains.

views.description: Most recent order per customer with order metadata. Exposes a row_number rank so callers can select the latest or top-N orders per customer. | Use for: latest order for each customer; recent order cohorts; top-N recent orders per customer

views.name: picking_activity_window
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  pl.picklist_id AS picklist_id,
  pl.log_time AS log_time,
  pl.activity AS activity,
  pl.location_id AS location_id,
  pl.pickline_no AS pickline_no,
  LAG(pl.log_time) OVER (PARTITION BY pl.picklist_id ORDER BY pl.log_time) AS prev_log_time,
  LEAD(pl.log_time) OVER (PARTITION BY pl.picklist_id ORDER BY pl.log_time) AS next_log_time,
  ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY pl.picklist_id ORDER BY pl.log_time) AS seq_in_picklist,
  COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY pl.picklist_id) AS total_events_in_picklist
FROM picking_log pl

params.when_to_use: Analyze events inside a single picklist at the event timestamp (log_time) — e.g., "show the sequence of activities for picklist 123". | Compute per-event metrics that depend on neighboring events in the same picklist, such as time since previous event or time until next event (uses prev_log_time/next_log_time). | Order or paginate events within a picklist using seq_in_picklist to reconstruct the activity sequence. | Count or report the total number of events for each picklist using total_events_in_picklist while still keeping each event row separate. | Filter or inspect activity-level attributes (activity, location_id, pickline_no) at the exact log_time for each event.
params.when_not_to_use: Do not use when you need picklist-level aggregated summaries (e.g., total pick duration, unique locations visited per picklist) — this view is at the event (picklist_id, log_time) grain and will return multiple rows per picklist; aggregating without caution can double-count or mis-count events. | Do not use when you need current/latest event per picklist unless you explicitly select the row with LEAD or ROW_NUMBER = max/1 — reusing the view directly may return past events as if they were the latest. | Do not use for cohort filters that operate at a different grain (for example, "picklists handled by employee X" if employee is stored elsewhere) — the view contains no worker/employee identifier, so joining/ filtering by that cohort requires additional joins and may produce incorrect cohorts if joined incorrectly. | Do not use when you need deduplicated picklist-level records (one row per picklist) — selecting DISTINCT picklist_id from this view loses event timing details and may hide which event corresponds to other aggregates like total_events_in_picklist. | Do not use to produce metrics that assume contiguous events without gaps unless you explicitly check prev_log_time/next_log_time — gaps are not collapsed or annotated beyond the raw neighboring timestamps. | Do not use when you need event counts for arbitrary windows (e.g., 1-hour windows across the warehouse) because partitioning and window functions are restricted to partition BY picklist_id; reuse could give misleading counts if you try to pivot to different aggregation scopes without re-deriving counts at that scope.
params.comparison: use orders_with_lines instead when you need join-based enrichment at the order/line grain — orders_with_lines provides order-level and line-level joins; picking_activity_window is event-log grain and lacks order/line attributes. | use product_monthly_sales or product_total_sales instead when you need aggregated sales metrics at product/time rollups — those AGG siblings provide pre-aggregated totals, whereas this view exposes event-level rows and per-picklist windowed columns which are irrelevant for product sales aggregation. | use orders_latest_by_customer instead when you need the latest record per entity (customer/order) — that sibling is designed to return the most recent row per partition using ranking logic; picking_activity_window returns all event rows per picklist and requires additional filtering to simulate 'latest'. | use inventory_with_locations or products_with_group when you need enriched master data (locations, product groups) via joins — those JOIN siblings provide stable dimensional attributes; picking_activity_window only surfaces location_id at the event timestamp and does not perform enrichment to product or inventory dimensions. | use web_daily_devices or web_demographics_unpivot when you need normalized or reshaped time-series or demographic data — those siblings are explicitly reshaped/normalized for analytics; picking_activity_window preserves raw event sequencing and is not transformed for aggregate time-series analysis.

views.description: Ordered picking_log events per picklist with lag/lead and a running count. Useful for analyzing picklist workflows, durations between activities, and sequence patterns. | Use for: time between pick events; sequence analysis of picking activities; identify first/last activity per picklist

views.name: employee_supervision_paths
views.body_sql:
SELECT id AS emp_id, name AS name, supervisor_id AS supervisor_id, 0 AS depth, CAST(id AS TEXT) AS path_ids
FROM employees
WHERE supervisor_id IS NULL
UNION ALL
SELECT e.id AS emp_id, e.name AS name, e.supervisor_id AS supervisor_id, esp.depth + 1 AS depth, esp.path_ids || '>' || CAST(e.id AS TEXT) AS path_ids
FROM employees e
JOIN employee_supervision_paths esp ON e.supervisor_id = esp.emp_id

params.when_to_use: To list every employee together with each distinct supervision distance (depth) from a root-level supervisor: e.g., “show all employees and the chain length from their top-level supervisor,” because the view emits one row per (emp_id, depth). | To reconstruct the supervision chain path as a separator-delimited string of IDs for each employee at each depth level, for purposes like displaying or exporting hierarchical paths. | To traverse the hierarchy from top-level supervisors downward (root-to-leaf traversal), because the recursive CTE seeds with supervisor_id IS NULL and grows children via JOIN on supervisor_id = esp.emp_id.
params.when_not_to_use: When you need one canonical row per employee (employee-level grain): the view intentionally emits multiple rows for the same emp_id at different depths, so aggregations or counts over this view will overcount employees unless you first reduce to a single depth per emp_id. | When you need supervision paths that start from an arbitrary ancestor (not a NULL supervisor): the recursion always seeds from rows with supervisor_id IS NULL, so it only builds paths rooted at top-level supervisors and will omit paths originating from non-root ancestors. | When you need the ordered list of ancestor IDs as an array or another structured type: path_ids is a text concatenation using '>' separators; treating it as an array or assuming numeric ordering will be fragile and require parsing. | When you need to filter by a cohort defined in the base employees table using conditions on non-selected columns: the view selects only id, name, supervisor_id; if your cohort depends on other employee columns that are not available, applying filters late against the view may be impossible or inefficient. | When you need the nearest/matching supervisor at a single level (e.g., only direct manager): the view includes rows at depth=0 for root supervisors and depth=1 for direct reports, but it also includes deeper depths — using it without restricting depth can produce incorrect matches for single-level questions. | When you need performance-sensitive incremental joins that expect a single-row-per-employee natural key: because the view exposes multiple rows per employee, joining it naively can multiply rows in downstream aggregations or cause unintended Cartesian-like expansions.
params.comparison: use orders_latest_by_customer instead when you need the single most-recent element per key — it is a RANK-style view designed to select one row per grouping; employee_supervision_paths is recursive and emits multiple rows per emp_id at different depths. | use products_with_group or products_with_alcohol instead when you need straightforward enriched attributes of a single product row — those JOIN views preserve one row per product, whereas employee_supervision_paths preserves multiple rows per employee and encodes hierarchy as a path string. | use product_total_sales or product_monthly_sales instead when you need aggregated metrics at a stable aggregation grain — those AGG views consolidate rows to the correct aggregation level, while employee_supervision_paths intentionally preserves multiple granular rows (different depths) and is not an aggregation view. | use web_demographics_unpivot or web_daily_devices when you need reshaped or normalized representations intended for analytics consumption — those sibling views change shape or normalize data but are explicit about their grain; employee_supervision_paths is recursive/hierarchical and must be treated as emitting one row per (emp_id, depth).

views.description: Recursive hierarchy of employee -> supervisor paths. Produces one row per employee-ancestor pair with depth. Useful for org-chart traversals and reporting up the management chain. | Use for: reporting chain for an employee; compute levels between employees and supervisors; build full org paths for visualization

views.name: product_reorder_guidance
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  p.id AS id,
  p.name AS name,
  COALESCE(SUM(i.qty),0) AS available_qty,
  pm.qty_minimum AS qty_minimum,
  pm.qty_purchase AS qty_purchase
FROM products p
LEFT JOIN inventory i ON p.id = i.product_id
LEFT JOIN product_minimums pm ON p.id = pm.product_id
GROUP BY p.id, p.name, pm.qty_minimum, pm.qty_purchase

params.when_to_use: When you need per-product static reorder guidance that combines the product row with the current summed on-hand quantity across all inventory records: returns one row per product (product id) with its name, total available_qty, and the product's configured minimum and purchase quantities. | When you want to list all products (including those with no inventory rows) together with their total available quantity (0 when no inventory) and the configured minimum/purchase amounts from product_minimums. | When you need to compute decisions or comparisons at the product-level (e.g., available_qty < qty_minimum) to flag products that may need reordering, using totals across inventory rows.
params.when_not_to_use: Do not use this view if you need inventory at the inventory-row or location level (e.g., per-warehouse or per-location quantities). This view aggregates inventory via SUM(i.qty) and returns a single available_qty per product, so location detail is lost and reusing it will silently hide distribution of stock. | Do not use this view when you need time-aware or historical available quantities (e.g., available at a given date or over time). The view aggregates current inventory rows without any date/time context — using it for past/future snapshots will produce incorrect results. | Do not use this view for queries that require the raw inventory rows (e.g., counting inventory records, computing medians, or joining by inventory id). Because inventory rows are aggregated, row-level counts and row identities are lost and any join expecting inventory ids will be wrong. | Avoid using this view when product_minimums can have multiple rows per product (effective-dated or multi-sourced) and you need to control which minimum/purchase row to use. The view GROUPs by pm.qty_minimum and pm.qty_purchase and will produce multiple product rows if multiple distinct (qty_minimum, qty_purchase) exist; conversely, if the intent is to pick the latest/active minimum, this view does not do that and will produce ambiguous results. | Do not reuse this view when you need sales/consumption-based reorder calculations (e.g., reorder point based on monthly sales). This view has no sales/consumption data — use an aggregated sales view instead. | Do not use this view when you need to filter to only products with inventory records (inner-join semantics). This view uses a LEFT JOIN to inventory and will include products with zero available_qty (COALESCE to 0), so queries expecting only stocked products will get extra rows unless you filter them out.
params.comparison: use inventory_with_locations instead when you need per-location or per-inventory-row quantities — inventory_with_locations preserves inventory row and location detail whereas product_reorder_guidance returns only per-product summed available_qty. | use product_total_sales or product_monthly_sales instead when reorder logic depends on sales volume or velocity — those AGG views provide sales totals or monthly aggregates; product_reorder_guidance contains no sales information. | use purchases_enriched or orders_with_lines when you need procurement or demand-side details tied to purchase/order lines — product_reorder_guidance is focused on on-hand quantity and configured minima, not on open purchase/order quantities. | use products_with_group or products_with_alcohol when you need product attribute joins (grouping, alcohol flag) — those JOIN views contain additional product attributes that product_reorder_guidance does not include. | use orders_latest_by_customer or web_daily_devices etc. only for their respective analytical purposes — these sibling views serve different grains and purposes (ranked/customer/device/time) and should not replace product-level inventory aggregations.

views.description: Per-product current inventory quantity and minimum/purchase rules to support reorder decisions. Exposes aggregated available_qty and compares to qty_minimum and qty_purchase. Use as input to reorder alerts and recommended purchase sizes. | Use for: which products need reorder; compute reorder quantity based on minimums; join reorder guidance to suppliers or purchases
